intro: Stars in a galaxy never collide: they move in the smooth potential of everyone else. Here you read a rotation curve, build a Plummer sphere from its distribution function, and use scaling arguments to weigh a galaxy cluster from its X-rays.

blocks.html: Edge-on, the Galaxy is a thin disk (radius ~15 kpc, thickness a few hundred pc, gas, dust, young stars, spiral arms) around a central bulge (a few kpc, old stars, a bar, and a $4\times10^6M_\odot$ black hole, Sgr A*), embedded in a nearly spherical stellar halo (globular clusters, old metal-poor stars) and a much larger dark-matter halo. The Sun sits in the disk about 8 kpc from the centre, moving at ~220 km/s, one orbit per ~230 Myr.

Population I: young, metal-rich stars in the disk, formed from gas enriched by earlier generations. Population II: old, metal-poor stars in the halo and bulge (and globular clusters), formed early before the gas was enriched.

Dynamical support: the disk is supported by rotation (stars on nearly circular orbits, small random velocities); the bulge and halo are supported by random motions (like a hot gas: velocity dispersion balances gravity via the virial theorem).

Metallicity is a clock: each generation of stars returns heavy elements to the ISM, so later stars are born metal-richer. Shapley (1918) located the centre of the Galaxy by noting that globular clusters (halo objects) are concentrated towards Sagittarius: the Sun is not at the centre.
Population numbering is "historical": Pop I = young and metal-rich (disk), Pop II = old and metal-poor (halo/bulge). Exams ask exactly this in MC every year.

options: old, metal-poor, in the halo and bulge

encounters.title: Galactic rotation and the case for dark matter

blocks.label: Circular velocity from the enclosed mass (spherical approximation).

blocks.html: If all the mass were the visible stars, concentrated in the inner few kpc, $v_c$ would fall as $r^{-1/2}$ (Keplerian) outside. 21 cm observations show flat rotation curves far beyond the visible disk: $v_c\approx$ const, so $M_r\propto r$ and $\rho\propto r^{-2}$. Most of the mass is dark.

blocks.label: Flat rotation curve, its density, and the escape speed for a halo truncated at R (HS25 practice Q6).

blocks.html: Near the Sun, differential rotation shows up in the radial and tangential velocities of nearby stars: $v_R=Ad\sin2l$, $v_T=Ad\cos2l+Bd$ with the Oort constants $A=14.8$, $B=-12.4$ km s$^{-1}$kpc$^{-1}$; $v_c(R_0)=(A-B)R_0$.

A flat rotation curve is the signature of a singular isothermal sphere (next lesson): a halo whose "particles" (dark matter) have the same velocity dispersion everywhere. The extra mass keeps the outer stars on fast orbits that visible matter alone could not hold.

Keep $M_r\propto r$ (flat curve) and $\rho\propto r^{-2}$ apart: MC asks both (HS25 winter MC12: $M_r\propto r$; HS24 summer MC13: $\rho\propto r^{-2}$). With a central black hole plus an $r^{-2}$ halo, $M_r=kr+M_0$ and $v^2=G(k+M_0/r)$ (HS24 winter Q4).

encounters.title: Why galaxies are collisionless: relaxation times

source.where: Choudhuri §7.3, eqs. (7.10)-(7.14), Table 7.1; violent relaxation; dynamical friction §7.4

blocks.html: A "collision" between stars is an encounter that changes a star's velocity by order itself. That needs an impact parameter $b\approx Gm/v^2$ (7.10). The time between such encounters:

blocks.label: (7.14). Binney & Tremaine refine this to N/(8 ln N).

blocks.html: Galaxy: $v\approx100$ km/s, $n\approx0.1$ pc$^{-3}$ gives $T_{\rm rel}\sim10^{17}$ yr: collisions are irrelevant; stars move in the smooth mean potential (collisionless). Globular clusters ($v\approx10$, $n\approx10^3$): $10^{10}$ yr, partially relaxed. Yet galaxies look relaxed: during formation the potential changes violently and stars exchange energy with the changing field (violent relaxation, Lynden-Bell 1967) within a few crossing times: $T_{\rm rel}\gg T_{VR}\gtrsim T_{\rm cross}$.

Dynamical friction: a massive body moving through a sea of stars pulls them towards itself; by the time they gather it has moved on, leaving an overdense wake behind it, whose gravity slows it down. This makes satellite galaxies and globular clusters spiral inwards.

Self-gravitating systems never reach true thermodynamic equilibrium: a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution in a self-consistent potential needs $\rho\propto r^{-2}$ at large $r$, i.e. infinite mass (Choudhuri §7.4). They relax by other (collective) processes to states that are not thermal equilibrium (HS24 winter MC11).

encounters.title: Distribution functions, Jeans equations and the isothermal sphere

blocks.html: A collisionless system is described by a distribution function $f(\mathbf x,\mathbf v,t)$ (stars per $d^3x\,d^3v$). Stars are conserved and move smoothly in phase space, so $f$ is constant along orbits: the collisionless Boltzmann (Vlasov) equation

abla^2\Phi=4\pi Gho

blocks.html: Jeans theorem: any function of the integrals of motion (energy $\mathcal E=\frac12v^2+\Phi$, angular momentum) solves it in a steady state. Choose $f(\mathcal E)$ and you have a model: e.g. $f\propto(-\mathcal E)^{7/2}$ gives the Plummer sphere $\rho\propto(-\Phi)^5$ (boss of this room).

Taking velocity moments gives the Jeans equations, the stellar analogue of hydrostatic equilibrium with "pressure" $\rho\sigma^2$. Spherical, isotropic: $\frac{d(\rho\sigma^2)}{dr}=-\rho\frac{GM_r}{r^2}$. With $\sigma$ constant (isothermal) a solution is the singular isothermal sphere:

blocks.label: Flat rotation curve; ⟨v²⟩ = 3σ² is independent of r (HS25 practice MC12).

blocks.html: The isothermal sphere is literally an isothermal self-gravitating gas: "temperature" = velocity dispersion. It explains flat rotation curves with one number $\sigma$, but its mass diverges ($M_r\propto r$), so real halos must be truncated (HS25 practice Q6) or steepen (NFW profiles).

encounters.title: Escape velocity from a truncated flat-rotation-curve halo
encounters.goal: For $\rho\propto r^{-2}$ out to a cut-off radius $R$ (zero beyond), show that $v_{esc}^2=2v_c^2\left(1+\ln\frac Rr\right)$ for $r<R$.

encounters.title: Singular isothermal sphere from the Jeans equation

source.where: Choudhuri §7.6 (spherical isotropic Jeans equation) and HS25 practice MC12

encounters.goal: With $\frac{d(\rho\sigma^2)}{dr}=-\rho\frac{GM_r}{r^2}$ and constant $\sigma$, show that $\rho=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\pi Gr^2}$ is a solution and that $v_c^2=2\sigma^2$.

steps.reveal: $M_r=4\pi Ar$. Left side: $\sigma^2\frac{d}{dr}\frac{A}{r^2}=-\frac{2\sigma^2A}{r^3}$. Right side: $-\frac{A}{r^2}\frac{G4\pi Ar}{r^2}=-\frac{4\pi GA^2}{r^3}$.

encounters.title: Weighing the Galaxy with a flat rotation curve
encounters.problem: The rotation curve is flat at $v_c=220$ km/s. Equating centripetal and gravitational acceleration, $v_c^2=GM_r/r$. Evaluate at $r=8$ kpc ($1$ kpc $=10^3$ pc).

steps.prompt: Mass density $\rho=v_c^2/(4\pi Gr^2)$ (from $M_r=4\pi\int r^2\rho\,dr\propto r$, i.e. $\rho\propto r^{-2}$) in $M_\odot/\text{pc}^3$.
steps.hint: Differentiate $M_r=v_c^2r/G$: $dM/dr=4\pi r^2\rho=v_c^2/G$. Then convert kg/m$^3$ to $M_\odot$/pc$^3$ with $pc^3/M_\odot$.

encounters.title: Dust towards the Galactic centre
encounters.problem: Toy model $n_H\propto\exp[-(r/r_0)^2]$, $r(s)=\sqrt{d^2+s^2-2ds\cos b}$ with $d=8$ kpc, $r_0=1.2$ kpc, and $A_V(b=0)=30$. The Gaussian integral gives $A_V(b)=30\exp\left[\frac{d^2}{r_0^2}(\cos^2b-1)\right]$.

steps.prompt: Flux ratio $F_{\rm ext}/F_0$ with $A_V=m_{\rm ext}-m_0=2.5\log_{10}(F_0/F_{\rm ext})$.

encounters.title: Scaling a galaxy cluster from its X-rays
encounters.problem: Thermal bremsstrahlung: $L_X\propto\int\rho_g^2T^{1/2}dV$. Virial equilibrium with thermal support gives $T\propto M/\langle R\rangle$; with $M\propto\langle R\rangle^3$ and $M_g=f_gM$ this gives $T\propto M^{2/3}$ and $L_X\propto M^{4/3}$. A cluster is 8 times more massive than another with the same gas fraction.

steps.hint: $\rho_g^2\propto R^{-6}M^2=M^0$ (constant), times $T^{1/2}\propto M^{1/3}$, times volume $\propto M$: $L_X\propto M^{4/3}$. $8^{4/3}=16$.

steps.prompt: Circular speed of the Sun $v_c=(A-B)R_0$ in km/s.

steps.hint: Convert kpc to km; about 230 Myr: the Sun has orbited ~20 times.

encounters.title: Boss: the Plummer sphere (exam problem)

source.where: Open Question 4 [Plummer sphere, 14 pt], HS25 winter session

encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer, then enter the final numbers. Part (a) is graded by you against the key points.
statement: A Plummer sphere is a collisionless stellar system of self-gravitating particles of mass $m$, spherically symmetric, with distribution function $f(\mathcal{E})=f_0(-\mathcal{E})^{7/2}$ for $\mathcal{E}<0$ and $0$ for $\mathcal{E}\ge0$, where $\mathcal{E}=v^2/2+\Phi(r)$ is the energy per unit mass.

(a) [6 pt] Show that the mass density $\rho(\Phi)\propto(-\Phi)^5$. Hints: $\rho(r)=4\pi m\int_0^{v_{\max}}f_0(-\mathcal{E})^{7/2}v^2dv$; relate $v_{\max}$ to $\Phi$; define $x=v^2/(-2\Phi)$; note $\int_0^1x^{1/2}(1-x)^{7/2}dx=7\pi/256$.
(b) [4 pt] With $\Phi(r)=-GM/\sqrt{r^2+a^2}$ (no derivation needed), find the circular velocity profile $v_c(r)$.
(c) [4 pt] With the Poisson equation $\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{d}{dr}(r^2\frac{d\Phi}{dr})=4\pi G\rho$, derive $\rho(r)$ and the central density.

finalAnswers.prompt: Part (b): $v_c$ at $r=a$ for $M=10^{11}M_\odot$, $a=1$ kpc, in km/s.
Part (c): the central density $3M/(4\pi a^3)$ for the same $M$, $a$, in $M_\odot/\text{pc}^3$.

keyPoints: (a) $\mathcal{E}<0\Leftrightarrow v<v_{\max}=\sqrt{-2\Phi}$. With $x=v^2/(-2\Phi)$: $-\mathcal{E}=-\Phi(1-x)$, $v=\sqrt{-2\Phi x}$, $dv=\sqrt{-\Phi/2}\,x^{-1/2}dx$. Then $\rho=4\sqrt2\pi mf_0(-\Phi)^5\int_0^1x^{1/2}(1-x)^{7/2}dx=\frac{7\pi^2\sqrt2\,mf_0}{64}(-\Phi)^5$. Powers of $(-\Phi)$: $7/2+3/2=5$.

(c) $r^2\Phi'=GMr^3/(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}$; derivative: $3GMa^2r^2/(r^2+a^2)^{5/2}$. Hence $\rho=\frac{3M}{4\pi a^3}(1+r^2/a^2)^{-5/2}$, $\rho(0)=\frac{3M}{4\pi a^3}$. Consistent with (a): $\rho\propto(r^2+a^2)^{-5/2}\propto(-\Phi)^5$.

encounters.title: Boss: a black hole inside an r⁻² halo (exam problem)
encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer, then enter the final number for (c). Parts (a)-(b) are graded by you against the key points.
statement: Let us build a simple model of a spherically symmetric galaxy. Assume that a point mass (a black hole) of mass $M_0=4\times10^6M_\odot$ is located at the centre of the galaxy ($r=0$) and that the remainder of the mass has a density profile that decays as $r^{-2}$, where $r$ is the radial distance from the galaxy centre.
(a) [4 pt] Show that the enclosed mass within a spherical region of radius $r$ can be expressed as $M_r=kr+M_0$, where $k$ is a constant to be determined later.
(b) [4 pt] Assuming circular motion and Newtonian gravity, show that the orbital velocity of a star at radius $r$ is $v=\left[G\left(k+\frac{M_0}{r}\right)\right]^{1/2}$.
(c) [4 pt] If the orbital velocity is 110 km s$^{-1}$ at 2 pc, determine the value of $k$ in units of $M_\odot$ pc$^{-1}$.
